replies.text: {"sentence": "According to the IPCC, limiting human-caused global warming requires net zero CO2 emissions; cumulative carbon emissions until net zero is reached and the level of greenhouse gas emission reductions this decade largely determine whether warming can be limited to 1.5°C or 2°C (high confidence), and projected CO2 emissions from existing fossil fuel infrastructure without additional abatement would exceed the remaining carbon budget for 1.5°C (50%) (high confidence)."}

{"sentence": "According to the IPCC, from a physical science perspective, limiting human-caused global warming to a specific level requires limiting cumulative CO2 emissions, reaching at least net zero CO2 emissions, and strongly reducing other greenhouse gas emissions; reaching net zero GHG emissions primarily requires deep reductions in CO2, methane, and other GHGs and implies net negative CO2 emissions, for which carbon dioxide removal will be necessary, and net zero GHG emissions, if sustained, are projected to result in a gradual decline in global surface temperatures after an earlier peak (high confidence)."}

{"sentence": "According to the IPCC (AR6 Synthesis Report, B.5.3), if annual CO2 emissions between 2020–2030 stayed, on average, at the 2019 level, cumulative emissions would almost exhaust the remaining carbon budget for 1.5°C (50%) and deplete more than a third of the remaining carbon budget for 2°C (67%); estimates of future CO2 emissions from existing fossil fuel infrastructure without additional abatement already exceed the remaining carbon budget for limiting warming to 1.5°C (50%) (high confidence); and projected cumulative future CO2 emissions over the lifetime of existing and planned fossil fuel infrastructure, if historical operating patterns are maintained and without additional abatement, are approximately equal to the remaining carbon budget for limiting warming to 2°C with a likelihood of 83% (high confidence)."}

{"sentence": "According to the IPCC's AR6 Synthesis Report (statement B.6), all global modelled pathways that limit warming to 1.5°C (>50%) with no or limited overshoot, and those that limit warming to 2°C (>67%), involve rapid and deep and, in most cases, immediate greenhouse gas emissions reductions in all sectors this decade, with global net zero CO2 emissions reached in the early 2050s and around the early 2070s respectively (high confidence)."}

{"sentence": "According to the IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report (B.6.1), global modelled pathways that limit warming to 1.5°C (>50%) with no or limited overshoot, or to 2°C (>67%) with immediate action, are characterized by deep, rapid, and in most cases immediate GHG emissions reductions, with global GHG emissions projected to peak between 2020 and at the latest before 2025, and with net zero CO2 reached in the early 2050s for 1.5°C pathways (followed by net negative CO2 emissions) and in the early 2070s for 2°C pathways, all stated with high confidence."}

{"sentence": "According to the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report Synthesis Report (statement B.6.3), global modelled mitigation pathways reaching net zero CO2 and GHG emissions include transitioning from fossil fuels without carbon capture and storage (CCS) to very low- or zero-carbon energy sources (such as renewables or fossil fuels with CCS), demand-side measures and improving efficiency, reducing non-CO2 GHG emissions, and carbon dioxide removal (CDR), and in most global modelled pathways, land-use change and forestry (via reforestation and reduced deforestation) and the energy supply sector reach net zero CO2 emissions earlier than the buildings, industry and transport sectors (high confidence)."}

{"sentence": "According to the IPCC (AR6 Synthesis Report, B.6.4), mitigation options often have synergies with other aspects of sustainable development but some can also have trade-offs: energy efficiency and renewable energy have potential synergies with sustainable development, and, depending on context, biological CDR methods such as reforestation, improved forest management, soil carbon sequestration, peatland restoration and coastal blue carbon management can enhance biodiversity and ecosystem functions, employment and local livelihoods, whereas afforestation or biomass crop production can have adverse socio-economic and environmental impacts, including on biodiversity, food and water security, local livelihoods and the rights of Indigenous Peoples, especially if implemented at large scales and where land tenure is insecure, while modelled pathways that use resources more efficiently or shift global development towards sustainability face fewer challenges, such as less dependence on CDR and less pressure on land and biodiversity (high confidence)."}
